name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q01 - Current scientific definition of hormones

questiontext.text: According to the current scientific definition, hormones are best described as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The classical definition of hormones has been expanded to include chemical messengers beyond those produced only by organised endocrine glands.

Step 2: Evaluation
Scientifically, hormones are defined as non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals acting as intercellular messengers and produced in trace amounts.

answer.text: Non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts
Nutrient chemicals produced in large quantities by exocrine glands
Structural proteins released through ducts to act only at the site of synthesis
Inorganic ions transported exclusively by nerve fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q02 - Organised endocrine bodies in humans

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT classified as an organised endocrine body in the human body, though it still produces hormones?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human endocrine system consists of organised endocrine glands as well as hormone-producing diffused tissues or cells in other organs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus, and gonads (testis and ovary) are the organised endocrine bodies. Organs such as the gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney, and heart also produce hormones, though they are not organised endocrine glands.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The kidney produces hormones (such as erythropoietin) but is not classified among the organised endocrine bodies.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q03 - Anatomical location of the pituitary gland

questiontext.text: The pituitary gland is located in a bony cavity called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pituitary gland lies at the base of the brain, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk.

Step 2: Evaluation
Anatomically, the pituitary gland sits inside a protective bony cavity known as the sella tursica.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The bony cavity housing the pituitary gland is the sella tursica.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q04 - Hormone secreted by pars intermedia

questiontext.text: Which single hormone is secreted by the pars intermedia of the adenohypophysis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adenohypophysis consists of two portions: pars distalis and pars intermedia.

Step 2: Evaluation
While pars distalis produces six trophic hormones (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, and FSH), pars intermedia secretes only one hormone, melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH), which regulates skin pigmentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH) is the sole hormone secreted by the pars intermedia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q05 - Pineal gland location and hormone

questiontext.text: The pineal gland is located on the dorsal side of the forebrain and secretes:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pineal gland regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the human body.

Step 2: Evaluation
Located on the dorsal side of the forebrain, the pineal gland secretes melatonin, which maintains normal rhythms of the sleep-wake cycle and body temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q06 - Structure connecting the two thyroid lobes

questiontext.text: The two lobes of the thyroid gland located on either side of the trachea are interconnected by a thin flap of connective tissue called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The thyroid gland is a bilobed structure positioned on either side of the trachea.

Step 2: Evaluation
Both lobes of the thyroid gland are joined across the midline by a thin flap of connective tissue known as the isthmus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The connecting structure is called the isthmus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q07 - Number and location of parathyroid glands

questiontext.text: How many parathyroid glands are present in humans, and where are they located?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Parathyroid glands are small endocrine glands associated anatomically with the thyroid gland.

Step 2: Evaluation
In humans, four parathyroid glands are present on the back (dorsal) side of the thyroid gland, arranged as one pair in each of the two thyroid lobes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are four parathyroid glands located on the back side of the thyroid gland.

answer.text: Two glands, one on the anterior part of each kidney
Two glands, one on the ventral side of each thyroid lobe
Four glands, one pair each on the back side of the two lobes of the thyroid gland
Four glands, embedded within the thymus between the lungs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q08 - Main mineralocorticoid in the human body

questiontext.text: Which hormone is the main mineralocorticoid in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Corticoids secreted by the adrenal cortex that regulate the balance of water and electrolytes are called mineralocorticoids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid in our body, whereas cortisol is the main glucocorticoid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid in humans.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q09 - Pancreatic islet cells secreting insulin

questiontext.text: In the Islets of Langerhans of the human pancreas, insulin is secreted by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The endocrine pancreas consists of Islets of Langerhans containing two main types of cells: \(\alpha\)-cells and \(\beta\)-cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
The \(\alpha\)-cells secrete glucagon, while the \(\beta\)-cells secrete insulin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Insulin is secreted by the \(\beta\)-cells of the Islets of Langerhans.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q10 - Androgen-producing cells in testis

questiontext.text: Which cells present in the intertubular spaces of the testis produce androgens, mainly testosterone?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The testis is composed of seminiferous tubules and stromal or interstitial tissue.

Step 2: Evaluation
The Leydig cells (also called interstitial cells) located in the intertubular spaces produce a group of hormones called androgens, mainly testosterone.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Leydig cells (interstitial cells) produce androgens in the testis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q11 - Hypothalamic inhibiting hormone for growth hormone

questiontext.text: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits the release of growth hormone from the pituitary gland?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The hypothalamus produces two types of hormones regulating the pituitary: releasing hormones and inhibiting hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulates the synthesis and release of gonadotrophins, whereas somatostatin from the hypothalamus inhibits the release of growth hormone from the pituitary.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Somatostatin inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q12 - Portal circulation between hypothalamus and anterior pituitary

questiontext.text: How do hypothalamic releasing and inhibiting hormones reach the anterior pituitary after being released from hypothalamic nerve endings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The hypothalamus regulates the anterior pituitary humorally and the posterior pituitary neurally.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hormones originating in hypothalamic neurons pass through axons, are released from their nerve endings, and reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system. In contrast, the posterior pituitary is under direct neural regulation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary through a portal circulatory system.

answer.text: Through exocrine ducts connecting the forebrain to the sella tursica
By direct axonal transport into the pars distalis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q13 - Acromegaly from adult growth hormone excess

questiontext.text: Excess secretion of growth hormone in adults, especially in middle age, results in severe disfigurement (particularly of the face) called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abnormalities in growth hormone (GH) secretion produce distinct disorders depending on age and whether secretion is excessive or deficient.

Step 2: Evaluation
Over-secretion of GH during growth leads to gigantism, and low secretion results in pituitary dwarfism. Excess secretion of GH in adults, especially in middle age, causes severe disfigurement (especially of the face) called acromegaly, which may lead to serious complications and premature death if unchecked.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adult-onset growth hormone excess causes acromegaly.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q14 - Role of luteinizing hormone in females

questiontext.text: In human females, which of the following is a primary function of luteinizing hormone (LH)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
LH and FSH are gonadotrophins secreted by the pars distalis that regulate gonadal activity in both sexes.

Step 2: Evaluation
In females, FSH stimulates growth and development of ovarian follicles, whereas LH induces ovulation of fully mature follicles (graafian follicles) and maintains the corpus luteum formed from the remnants of the graafian follicles after ovulation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
LH induces ovulation of graafian follicles and maintains the corpus luteum in females.

answer.text: Stimulating growth of mammary glands and milk formation
Inducing ovulation of graafian follicles and maintaining the corpus luteum
Regulating pigmentation of the skin via melanocytes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q15 - Actions of oxytocin on smooth muscles

questiontext.text: Which hormone acts on smooth muscles of the body to stimulate vigorous contraction of the uterus at childbirth and milk ejection from the mammary gland?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin.

Step 2: Evaluation
Oxytocin acts on smooth muscles and stimulates their contraction; in females, it triggers vigorous uterine contractions during childbirth and milk ejection from the mammary gland.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oxytocin is responsible for uterine contractions at childbirth and milk ejection.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q16 - Cause and features of Diabetes Insipidus

questiontext.text: An impairment affecting the synthesis or release of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) leads to a diminished ability of the kidney to conserve water, causing water loss and dehydration. This condition is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vasopressin (ADH) stimulates resorption of water and electrolytes by the distal renal tubules, reducing water loss through urine (diuresis).

Step 2: Evaluation
When ADH synthesis or release is impaired, the kidney cannot conserve water effectively, leading to water loss and dehydration. This condition is termed Diabetes Insipidus (distinct from diabetes mellitus, which involves prolonged hyperglycemia due to insulin deficiency/resistance).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ADH deficiency causes Diabetes Insipidus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q17 - Physiological roles of melatonin

questiontext.text: Besides regulating the 24-hour diurnal rhythm (sleep-wake cycle and body temperature), which set of functions is also influenced by melatonin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Melatonin secreted by the pineal gland has broad regulatory effects beyond circadian rhythm maintenance.

Step 2: Evaluation
In addition to maintaining sleep-wake cycles and body temperature, melatonin influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle, and our defense capability.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Melatonin influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle, and defense capability.

answer.text: Metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle, and defense capability
Bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and gastric HCl secretion
Glycogenesis, bile secretion, and uterine contraction at childbirth
Spermatogenesis, sodium reabsorption, and ketone body formation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q18 - Effects of hypothyroidism during pregnancy

questiontext.text: Hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby, leading to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thyroid hormones are essential for normal physical and neural development and maturation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hypothyroidism during pregnancy impairs fetal development and maturation, resulting in stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin, and deaf-mutism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Maternal hypothyroidism during pregnancy leads to cretinism, mental retardation, low IQ, abnormal skin, and deaf-mutism in the baby.

answer.text: Acromegaly, protrusion of eyeballs, and increased basal metabolic rate
Cretinism, mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin, and deaf-mutism
Gigantism, hyperglycemia, and formation of ketone bodies

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q19 - Features of Graves' disease

questiontext.text: Which set of clinical features characterises exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism caused by abnormally high synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation
It is characterised by enlargement of the thyroid gland, protrusion of the eyeballs, increased basal metabolic rate, and weight loss.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Graves' disease presents with thyroid enlargement, protruding eyeballs, elevated BMR, and weight loss.

answer.text: Decreased basal metabolic rate, weight gain, and irregular menstrual cycle
Enlargement of thyroid gland, protrusion of eyeballs, increased BMR, and weight loss
Acute weakness, fatigue, and altered carbohydrate metabolism due to adrenal cortex failure

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q20 - Thyrocalcitonin and blood calcium regulation

questiontext.text: In addition to \(\mathrm{T}_3\) and \(\mathrm{T}_4\), the thyroid gland secretes a protein hormone that regulates blood calcium levels by decreasing them. This hormone is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The thyroid gland secretes iodothyronines (\(\mathrm{T}_3\) and \(\mathrm{T}_4\)) as well as a calcium-regulating protein hormone.

Step 2: Evaluation
Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) is the protein hormone secreted by the thyroid gland that regulates blood calcium levels by decreasing them, acting alongside parathyroid hormone (PTH) in calcium homeostasis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) is the thyroid protein hormone that lowers blood calcium levels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q21 - Mechanisms by which PTH raises blood calcium

questiontext.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
PTH is a hypercalcemic peptide hormone whose secretion is regulated by circulating levels of calcium ions.

Step 2: Evaluation
PTH acts on bones to stimulate bone resorption (dissolution/demineralisation), stimulates reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) by the renal tubules, and increases \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) absorption from digested food.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
PTH elevates blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) via bone resorption, renal \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) reabsorption, and intestinal \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) absorption.

answer.text: Stimulating bone resorption, renal \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) reabsorption, and \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) absorption from digested food
Inhibiting bone demineralisation and increasing urinary \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) excretion
Stimulating glycogenesis in hepatocytes and inhibiting intestinal calcium uptake
Promoting \(\mathrm{K}^+\) reabsorption and \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) excretion in the renal tubules

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q22 - Role of thymosins in cell-mediated and humoral immunity

questiontext.text: Thymosins secreted by the thymus gland play a major role in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The thymus gland plays a major role in the development of the immune system by secreting peptide hormones called thymosins.

Step 2: Evaluation
Thymosins drive the differentiation of T-lymphocytes, which provide cell-mediated immunity, and also promote the production of antibodies to provide humoral immunity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thymosins support both cell-mediated immunity (T-lymphocyte differentiation) and humoral immunity (antibody production).

answer.text: Stimulating erythropoiesis in the kidney and bone resorption
Differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity) and promoting antibody production (humoral immunity)
Suppressing immune responses and producing anti-inflammatory reactions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q23 - Thymus degeneration and weakened immunity in old age

questiontext.text: Why do immune responses become weak in old individuals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thymosins are essential for T-lymphocyte differentiation and antibody production.

Step 2: Evaluation
In old individuals, the thymus gland degenerates, resulting in decreased production of thymosins. Consequently, their immune responses become weak.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Degeneration of the thymus in old age reduces thymosin production, weakening immune responses.

answer.text: Over-secretion of cortisol from the adrenal medulla
Hypertrophy of the pineal gland causing excess melatonin
Degeneration of the thymus gland leading to decreased production of thymosins
Deficiency of iodine in the diet reducing thyrocalcitonin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q24 - Addison's disease and adrenal cortex hyposecretion

questiontext.text: Underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, causing acute weakness and fatigue, and leads to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The adrenal cortex secretes corticoids, including glucocorticoids involved in carbohydrate metabolism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Underproduction of hormones by the adrenal cortex alters carbohydrate metabolism, resulting in acute weakness and fatigue—a condition known as Addison's disease.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adrenal cortex hyposecretion leads to Addison's disease.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q25 - Emergency hormones of the adrenal medulla

questiontext.text: Which pair of hormones is commonly called catecholamines or hormones of Fight or Flight?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The centrally located adrenal medulla secretes hormones rapidly in response to stress and emergency situations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine) are collectively called catecholamines, emergency hormones, or hormones of Fight or Flight.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adrenaline and noradrenaline are the catecholamines / Fight or Flight hormones.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q26 - Three histological layers of the adrenal cortex

questiontext.text: What is the correct order of the three layers of the adrenal cortex from the innermost layer to the outermost layer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The adrenal cortex is organised into three distinct concentric histological zones.

Step 2: Evaluation
From inner to outer, the three layers of the adrenal cortex are: zona reticularis (inner layer), zona fasciculata (middle layer), and zona glomerulosa (outer layer).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The inner-to-outer sequence is zona reticularis, zona fasciculata, and zona glomerulosa.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q27 - Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive action of cortisol

questiontext.text: Which hormone produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response, and also stimulates RBC production?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glucocorticoids, particularly cortisol, are steroid hormones secreted by the adrenal cortex.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cortisol is involved in maintaining cardiovascular and kidney functions, produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response, and stimulates RBC production.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cortisol produces anti-inflammatory reactions, suppresses the immune response, and stimulates RBC production.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q28 - Action of aldosterone on renal tubules

questiontext.text: Aldosterone acts mainly at the renal tubules to stimulate:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid regulating water and electrolyte balance.

Step 2: Evaluation
At the renal tubules, aldosterone stimulates the reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and water and the excretion of \(\mathrm{K}^+\) and phosphate ions, thereby maintaining electrolytes, body fluid volume, osmotic pressure, and blood pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aldosterone stimulates reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and water and excretion of \(\mathrm{K}^+\) and phosphate ions.

answer.text: Excretion of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and water, and reabsorption of \(\mathrm{K}^+\) ions
Reabsorption of glucose and excretion of \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) ions
Excretion of bicarbonate ions and reabsorption of urea
Reabsorption of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and water, and excretion of \(\mathrm{K}^+\) and phosphate ions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q29 - Hyperglycemic action of glucagon

questiontext.text: Glucagon acts mainly on liver cells (hepatocytes) to increase blood glucose levels by stimulating:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glucagon is a hyperglycemic peptide hormone secreted by \(\alpha\)-cells of the Islets of Langerhans.

Step 2: Evaluation
Glucagon acts mainly on hepatocytes and stimulates both glycogenolysis (breakdown of glycogen to glucose) and gluconeogenesis, while reducing cellular glucose uptake and utilisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in hepatocytes.

answer.text: Renal glucose excretion and ketone body clearance

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q30 - Target cells and actions of insulin

questiontext.text: Insulin lowers blood glucose levels (hypoglycemia) by acting mainly on:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insulin is a peptide hormone secreted by \(\beta\)-cells that plays a major role in glucose homeostasis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes (liver cells) and adipocytes (cells of adipose tissue), enhancing cellular glucose uptake and utilisation and stimulating the conversion of glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Insulin acts mainly on hepatocytes and adipocytes to enhance glucose uptake and glycogenesis.

answer.text: Renal distal tubules to increase water excretion
Hepatocytes and adipocytes to enhance cellular glucose uptake, utilisation, and glycogenesis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q31 - Clinical features of diabetes mellitus

questiontext.text: Prolonged hyperglycemia leads to diabetes mellitus, which is characteristically associated with:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insulin deficiency and/or insulin resistance results in prolonged hyperglycemia and the metabolic disorder diabetes mellitus.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diabetes mellitus is associated with loss of glucose through urine and the formation of harmful compounds known as ketone bodies; diabetic patients are successfully treated with insulin therapy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Diabetes mellitus is associated with urinary glucose loss and ketone body formation.

answer.text: Protrusion of eyeballs and elevated blood calcium
Loss of glucose through urine and formation of ketone bodies
Excessive secretion of ADH and water retention

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q32 - Sources of estrogen and progesterone in the ovary

questiontext.text: In the human ovary, estrogen and progesterone are synthesised and secreted mainly by which structures respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ovary produces two groups of steroid hormones: estrogen and progesterone.

Step 2: Evaluation
Estrogen is synthesised and secreted mainly by the growing ovarian follicles. After ovulation, the ruptured follicle is converted into a structure called the corpus luteum, which secretes mainly progesterone.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Estrogen is secreted mainly by growing ovarian follicles, and progesterone mainly by the corpus luteum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q33 - Atrial natriuretic factor and blood pressure reduction

questiontext.text: When blood pressure increases, the atrial wall of the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which reduces blood pressure by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is a peptide hormone secreted by the atrial wall of the heart.

Step 2: Evaluation
When blood pressure rises, ANF is secreted and causes dilation of the blood vessels, thereby decreasing blood pressure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ANF lowers blood pressure by causing dilation of blood vessels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q34 - Kidney juxtaglomerular cells and erythropoietin

questiontext.text: The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce a peptide hormone called erythropoietin, which stimulates:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Non-endocrine organs such as the kidney secrete peptide hormones with specific physiological targets.

Step 2: Evaluation
The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, which stimulates erythropoiesis (the formation of red blood cells).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Erythropoietin stimulates erythropoiesis (formation of RBCs).

answer.text: Secretion of bile juice from gall bladder

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q35 - Comparison of neural and endocrine coordination

questiontext.text: Why is endocrine coordination required in addition to the neural system in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The neural system and the endocrine system jointly coordinate and regulate physiological functions in the body.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neural coordination provides point-to-point rapid coordination that is fast but short-lived. Because nerve fibres do not innervate all cells of the body and cellular functions require continuous regulation, hormones provide the necessary sustained coordination and integration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Endocrine coordination is needed because neural coordination is short-lived and nerve fibres do not innervate all body cells.

answer.text: Neural coordination is slower and longer-lived than hormonal coordination
Hormones act only on cells directly innervated by motor neurons
Neural coordination is fast but short-lived, and nerve fibres do not innervate all cells of the body
Invertebrates lack neural systems and rely solely on complex endocrine glands

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q36 - Hormonal regulation of spermatogenesis in males

questiontext.text: In human males, which combination of hormones directly regulates the process of spermatogenesis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gonadotrophins (LH and FSH) from the anterior pituitary regulate testicular function.

Step 2: Evaluation
In males, LH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of androgens (mainly testosterone) from the testis. Together, FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis (formation of spermatozoa).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
FSH and androgens regulate spermatogenesis in males.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q37 - Structural and secretory organisation of the human pituitary

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the human pituitary gland?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pituitary gland is divided anatomically into adenohypophysis (pars distalis and pars intermedia) and neurohypophysis (pars nervosa).

Step 2: Evaluation
Pars distalis produces six trophic hormones (GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH). Pars intermedia secretes only one hormone (MSH) and, in humans, is almost merged with pars distalis. Neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin and vasopressin, which are synthesised by the hypothalamus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In humans, the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis, and the neurohypophysis stores and releases two hypothalamic hormones.

answer.text: In humans, pars intermedia is almost merged with pars distalis, and neurohypophysis stores and releases two hypothalamic hormones
Pars intermedia produces six trophic hormones whereas pars distalis secretes only MSH
Neurohypophysis synthesises oxytocin and vasopressin independently of the hypothalamus
Adenohypophysis is under direct neural regulation of the hypothalamus without any portal circulation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q38 - Distinguishing GH-related growth disorders

questiontext.text: Which comparison between gigantism, pituitary dwarfism, and acromegaly is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Growth hormone (GH) regulates somatic growth; its dysregulation produces distinct clinical outcomes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Over-secretion of GH stimulates abnormal body growth leading to gigantism, low secretion of GH results in stunted growth (pituitary dwarfism), and excess secretion of GH in adults (especially middle age) causes severe facial disfigurement known as acromegaly, which is hard to diagnose in early stages.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Gigantism and acromegaly both involve GH over-secretion (with acromegaly occurring in adults), whereas pituitary dwarfism results from low GH secretion.

answer.text: Acromegaly is caused by low GH secretion in childhood, whereas pituitary dwarfism is caused by adult GH excess
Gigantism results from GH over-secretion, pituitary dwarfism from low GH secretion, and acromegaly from excess GH in adults
Acromegaly is easily diagnosed in its earliest stages before any external feature changes appear
Pituitary dwarfism is caused by excess somatostatin inhibition of thyroid hormones

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q39 - Hormones supporting red blood cell formation

questiontext.text: Which of the following hormones does NOT support or stimulate the process of red blood cell (RBC) formation (erythropoiesis)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Several hormones in the human endocrine system support or stimulate erythropoiesis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Thyroid hormones support red blood cell formation; cortisol stimulates RBC production; erythropoietin from the kidney stimulates erythropoiesis; and androgens stimulate erythropoietic pathways. In contrast, parathyroid hormone (PTH) regulates blood calcium homeostasis and does not stimulate RBC formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) does not support or stimulate erythropoiesis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q40 - Calcium homeostasis by PTH and TCT

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly explains the regulation of blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) balance in the human body?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood calcium levels are maintained by the antagonistic actions of parathyroid hormone (PTH) and thyrocalcitonin (TCT).

Step 2: Evaluation
PTH is a hypercalcemic peptide hormone whose secretion is regulated by circulating \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels; it increases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and intestinal absorption. TCT is a protein hormone secreted by the thyroid gland that decreases blood calcium levels.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
PTH increases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels while TCT decreases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels, jointly maintaining calcium balance.

answer.text: Both PTH and TCT are hypercalcemic hormones secreted by the parathyroid glands
PTH secretion is stimulated exclusively by TSH from the anterior pituitary
TCT stimulates bone resorption to raise blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels
PTH increases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels (regulated by circulating \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\)), while TCT decreases blood \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) levels

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q41 - Metabolic effects of glucocorticoids

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately describes the metabolic actions of glucocorticoids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glucocorticoids from the adrenal cortex are primarily involved in carbohydrate, lipid, and protein metabolism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Glucocorticoids stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis, and they inhibit cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Glucocorticoids promote gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis while inhibiting cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids.

answer.text: They stimulate gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and proteolysis, and inhibit cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids
They stimulate glycogenesis and enhance cellular uptake and utilisation of amino acids
They inhibit gluconeogenesis and promote rapid movement of glucose into adipocytes
They stimulate protein synthesis in skeletal muscle and inhibit lipolysis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q42 - Hormones stimulating glycogen breakdown

questiontext.text: Which pair of hormones both stimulate the breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis), resulting in an increased concentration of glucose in the blood?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood glucose concentration can be raised by hormones that trigger glycogenolysis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Catecholamines (adrenaline and noradrenaline) from the adrenal medulla stimulate the breakdown of glycogen, increasing blood glucose concentration. Similarly, glucagon from pancreatic \(\alpha\)-cells stimulates glycogenolysis in hepatocytes, resulting in hyperglycemia.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adrenaline and glucagon both stimulate glycogenolysis to raise blood glucose levels.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q43 - Proportion of Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas

questiontext.text: In a normal human pancreas, approximately how many Islets of Langerhans are present, and what percentage of the pancreatic tissue do they represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pancreas is a composite gland functioning as both an exocrine and an endocrine gland.

Step 2: Evaluation
The endocrine portion consists of Islets of Langerhans; there are about 1 to 2 million Islets of Langerhans in a normal human pancreas, representing only 1 to 2 per cent of the pancreatic tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A normal human pancreas has about 1 to 2 million Islets of Langerhans, representing 1 to 2 per cent of pancreatic tissue.

answer.text: About 10 to 20 thousand islets, representing 10 to 20 per cent of pancreatic tissue
About 1 to 2 million islets, representing 25 to 30 per cent of pancreatic tissue
About 1 to 2 million islets, representing 1 to 2 per cent of pancreatic tissue
About 1 to 2 lakh islets, representing 5 to 10 per cent of pancreatic tissue

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q44 - Target organs of cholecystokinin

questiontext.text: Which gastrointestinal peptide hormone acts on both the pancreas and the gall bladder to stimulate the secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Endocrine cells in the gastrointestinal tract secrete four major peptide hormones: gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK), and gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP).

Step 2: Evaluation
Gastrin stimulates HCl and pepsinogen secretion; secretin stimulates water and bicarbonate ion secretion from the exocrine pancreas; GIP inhibits gastric secretion and motility; and cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on both the pancreas and gall bladder to stimulate secretion of pancreatic enzymes and bile juice, respectively.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cholecystokinin (CCK) acts on both the pancreas and gall bladder.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q45 - Inhibitory action of gastric inhibitory peptide

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about gastrointestinal hormones is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four major peptide hormones of the gastrointestinal tract have distinct stimulatory or inhibitory roles in digestion.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gastrin stimulates gastric glands to secrete HCl and pepsinogen. Secretin stimulates the exocrine pancreas to secrete water and bicarbonate ions. CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme and bile juice secretion. Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) inhibits—rather than stimulates—gastric secretion and motility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The claim that GIP stimulates gastric secretion and motility is incorrect, as GIP inhibits them.

answer.text: Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) stimulates gastric secretion and motility
Gastrin acts on gastric glands to stimulate secretion of HCl and pepsinogen
Secretin acts on the exocrine pancreas to stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate ions
Cholecystokinin acts on both pancreas and gall bladder

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q46 - Action of progesterone on mammary glands

questiontext.text: In addition to supporting pregnancy, progesterone acts on the mammary glands to stimulate:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mammary gland development, milk formation, milk storage, and milk ejection are regulated by distinct hormones (prolactin, estrogens, progesterone, and oxytocin).

Step 2: Evaluation
Progesterone supports pregnancy and acts on the mammary glands to stimulate the formation of alveoli (sac-like structures that store milk) and milk secretion. By contrast, oxytocin stimulates milk ejection, and prolactin regulates growth of mammary glands and milk formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Progesterone stimulates the formation of alveoli (which store milk) and milk secretion.

answer.text: Formation of alveoli (sac-like structures which store milk) and milk secretion

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q47 - Second messengers in membrane-bound receptor signalling

questiontext.text: Hormones that interact with membrane-bound receptors normally do not enter the target cell, but instead regulate cellular metabolism by generating second messengers such as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Peptide, polypeptide, protein hormones, and amino-acid derivatives bind to membrane-bound receptors on target cell membranes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because these hormones normally do not enter the target cell, hormone-receptor binding generates intracellular second messengers such as cyclic AMP (cAMP), \(\mathrm{IP}_3\), and \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\), which in turn regulate cellular metabolism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cyclic AMP, \(\mathrm{IP}_3\), and \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) act as second messengers in membrane-bound receptor signalling.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHEMICALCOORDINATIONANDINTEGRATION_MCQ_Q48 - Intracellular receptor mechanism of steroids and iodothyronines

questiontext.text: Which groups of hormones primarily interact with intracellular (mostly nuclear) receptors and regulate gene expression or chromosome function via interaction of the hormone-receptor complex with the genome?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hormone receptors are either membrane-bound or intracellular (mostly nuclear).

Step 2: Evaluation
Hormones that interact with intracellular receptors—such as steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone) and iodothyronines (thyroid hormones)—mostly regulate gene expression or chromosome function by the interaction of the hormone-receptor complex with the genome.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Steroid hormones and iodothyronines act via intracellular/nuclear receptors to regulate gene expression.

answer.text: Peptide hormones and amino-acid derivatives such as epinephrine
